analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain foreign swap deals of U.S.-owned banks from Dodd-Frank's derivatives rules.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House Financial Services Committee 41-18 but never received a vote in the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 crisis, the Dodd-Frank law required banks dealing in swaps — contracts whose value is tied to interest rates, currencies, or other assets — to meet capital, reporting, and trading rules. This bill would carve certain foreign deals out of those rules: swaps between a U.S.-owned bank and its own overseas branches or affiliates would be exempt if reported to regulators, and foreign banks would be allowed to follow their home countries' capital rules instead. Supporters said this prevented other countries' rules from being overridden by U.S. rules on trades made abroad; critics said it let banks shift risky derivatives business outside American oversight. The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee but was never voted on by the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and swap dealers — the Wall Street firms that trade derivatives — gain the most. A U.S.-owned bank's trades with its own foreign subsidiaries, branches, and affiliates would escape Dodd-Frank's Title VII rules (capital, margin, and clearing requirements) as long as the trades are reported to a data repository. Foreign banks registering as swap dealers could satisfy U.S. capital rules by meeting their home country's standards instead.

how_it_helps.text: It exempts swaps between U.S.-parented dealers and their own foreign branches, subsidiaries, and affiliates from Dodd-Frank Title VII, as long as the dealer reports the swap to a registered data repository — sparing those banks from applying U.S. swap rules to transactions booked abroad.
It lets registered foreign swap dealers satisfy Dodd-Frank capital requirements by complying with comparable home-country rules, so long as their country signed the Basel Accords.

It gives foreign-registered dealers legal certainty about which transactions U.S. rules cover, limiting their obligations to swaps made directly with a U.S. person outside the dealer's own affiliate network.

analysis.who_pays: Regulators' ability to police swaps loses ground: transactions routed through a bank's foreign affiliates would fall outside Dodd-Frank even when the parent is American, weakening the transparency and capital protections that were meant to keep derivatives risk from spreading through the financial system — the kind of risk that contributed to the 2008 crisis. Ordinary people bear that risk indirectly as taxpayers and as counterparties in a less transparent market.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weaker derivatives oversight

drawbacks.text: It exempts swaps between U.S.-parented dealers and their own foreign affiliates from Dodd-Frank's Title VII rules, reducing regulatory visibility into transactions those same banks could structure across borders; the bill relies only on a reporting requirement and a written anti-evasion rule to police the line.

It lets non-U.S. dealers meet Dodd-Frank capital standards by complying with their home country's rules instead, if those countries signed the Basel Accords — substituting foreign rules for American ones even when the foreign standards are weaker.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real problem — foreign regulators objected to Dodd-Frank reaching into their markets, and some deal routing was genuinely contested. But its mechanism, exempting the foreign transactions of U.S.-parented dealers from Dodd-Frank rules, would have opened a channel for swap activity to move offshore, to the benefit of the dealers and at some cost to the transparency that protects end-users and the broader financial system. It died without ever reaching a House vote, so no cost was actually incurred.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Financial Services Committee and was printed for House action, but the House never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended in January 2013, so it expired.

narrative.text: Introduced October 31, 2011 by Rep. James Himes, a Democrat, with Rep. Scott Garrett, a Republican, and referred to the Financial Services and Agriculture Committees.
The House Financial Services Committee approved it 41-18 on March 27, 2012 and reported it to the House on May 11, 2012.

The House Agriculture Committee kept extending its time to consider the bill — five extensions from May through December 2012 — before discharging it on December 14, 2012, when it was placed on the Union Calendar for possible House action.
The House never brought the bill to the floor for a vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street swap dealers are better off: the exemption limiting Dodd-Frank's reach to their foreign affiliate trades never became law, so those transactions remained fully subject to U.S. derivatives rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Swap-dealing banks; the exemption never passed

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and Republican lead, 15 cosponsors split 9 Democrats and 6 Republicans, and cleared committee 41-18 with votes from both parties, though 18 members voted no.

industries.note: The bill would relieve U.S.-parented banks from applying Dodd-Frank swap rules to trades with their own foreign affiliates, and let foreign dealers use home-country capital rules. For ordinary people this means less transparency and margin protection on a derivatives market implicated in the 2008 crisis.

industries.industry: Foreign banks and non-U.S. swap dealers
industries.note: Foreign dealers gain clear limits on when U.S. swap rules reach them and flexibility on capital standards, but must register and report trades with U.S. counterparties, and face an anti-evasion rule.
